The Story of Sudrishti the Goldsmith

I bow to Lord Jina, worshipped by gods, Vidyadharas, Chakravartins, kings, and maharajas, and I write the story of Sudrishti the goldsmith, who was very skilled in gem-work.

King Prajapal of Ujjain was devoted to the welfare of his subjects, righteous, and a true devotee of the Lord. His queen was Suprabha, who was very beautiful and chaste. Truly, only that beauty which is adorned with good conduct is worthy of praise.

In that city lived a goldsmith named Sudrishti. He was very skilled in gem-work, virtuous, and simple-natured. His wife was Vimla. Vimla was of bad conduct. She had an illicit relationship with a student named Vakra, whom Sudrishti was supporting and educating at his own expense. Vimla was very unhappy with her husband. So she incited her lover Vakra, giving him various good and bad advice, and had Sudrishti murdered. The murder was committed while Sudrishti was engaged in sensual pleasure. So he was reborn in Vimla's own womb.

After some days, Vimla gave birth to a son. The Acharyas say: the state of the world is very strange. In a single moment, through the subjection of karma, living beings undergo astonishing transformations. Like an actress, they change their form moment by moment.

It was the month of Chaitra. The beauty of spring had established its dominion everywhere. The beauty of forests and gardens captivated the mind. During this lovely season, one day Queen Suprabha was enjoying herself with her beloved lord in her special garden. In the course of play, her precious necklace called Kreedavilas broke, and all its gems scattered. The king tried hard to have it made exactly as before. He called goldsmiths from everywhere, but no one could recreate the necklace as it was. Truly, without the flower of practice, no one can know the highest art.

Vimla's son — that is, Sudrishti from his previous birth — saw the broken necklace. Seeing it, he remembered his past life. He recreated the necklace exactly as it had been before. The reason was that Sudrishti himself had made this necklace in his previous life. And it is true that skill in arts, knowledge, science, charity, worship — all these come to a soul only through the merit of past lives.

Seeing this miracle, the king was amazed. He asked the boy how he could recreate a necklace that no other goldsmith could match. The boy told the whole story of his past life — how he had been Sudrishti the goldsmith, how his wife Vimla had had him murdered, and how he had been reborn as her son. The king was deeply moved by this story of karma and rebirth. He developed faith in Jain dharma and became a devoted follower of Lord Jina.

The boy, through the memory of his past life and his skill in his art, eventually became a great goldsmith. But he also recognised the impermanence of worldly life. He renounced his profession, took initiation as a monk, and through dedicated spiritual practice, ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that the soul carries its skills and knowledge from life to life through the power of karma. Sudrishti's ability to recreate the necklace came from his past life's practice. The wise should understand that all abilities are the fruit of past merit, and they should use their skills not only for worldly success but also for spiritual progress.
